title: Why Your UI Style Guide Sucks
intro: Lightweight style guides show a button's colour, padding and maybe a hover state, then leave developers to invent the rest. A button has a dozen or more states, and each one is a UX decision someone will make — designed or not.

topics.title: Why Your UI Style Guide Sucks

learn.title: A button has more than three states
learn.text:
Typical Figma guide: default, hover, disabled, and “dev will figure out the rest”.

What a button actually needs:

• **focus-visible** and **pressed (active)**
• **selected**, plus selected + hover and selected + focus
• **loading** and indeterminate
• **error, warning, success, confirmation**

try.q: Which state does Calabro see skipped most often?
options: Pressed
Hover
Disabled
Focus-visible for keyboard users
try.explain: It is the user's immediate proof that something happened.

learn.title: Why combined states exist
learn.text:
People switch between mouse and keyboard mid-task. That produces states like **selected + focused** or **selected + hovered** that nobody specified.

**focus-visible** must be distinct from hover — keyboard and assistive-tech users rely on it.

**Loading** belongs on anything tied to a background process, with a **confirmation** (“Submitted”) afterwards.

try.q: Why must the focus style differ from the hover style?
options: Keyboard users rely on it to know where they are
Hover styles don't render on touch devices
Focus styles have stricter contrast requirements
Design systems usually define them separately
try.explain: Reusing the hover style leaves keyboard users without a position indicator.

learn.title: Who makes the decision if you don't
learn.text:
Visual values belong in tokens and CSS. **The guide's job is states and behaviour.**

When the guide says “you figure it out”, developers make interaction decisions without UX context — and the inconsistency shows up later as bugs, accessibility failures and components that behave differently in each part of the product.

try.q: What belongs in the style guide rather than in tokens?
options: States and behaviour
Hex values and spacing scales
Typography and font weights
Border radius and shadow depth
try.explain: Visual values live in tokens; the guide documents what the component does.

test.q: What is the real cost of an incomplete style guide?
options: Developers make UX decisions without context
Designers spend longer in review
Components take longer to build
The design system gradually falls out of date
test.explain: The inconsistency surfaces as bugs and accessibility failures.

test.q: What does the pressed state give the user?
options: Immediate proof the action registered
A preview of the resulting page
An indication that the control is still enabled
A visual match with the hover state

test.q: When should a button have a loading state?
options: Whenever it triggers a background process
Only on forms that submit to a server
Only when the expected wait exceeds five seconds
Whenever the design system provides one
Users switch between mouse and keyboard
Designers routinely forget to specify them
They are required by WCAG 2.2
They appear only in dark mode
test.explain: Selected + focused, selected + hovered and similar combinations occur in real use.

test.q: Which is a behaviour question rather than a visual one?
options: What happens while the action is processing
Which grey the disabled state uses
How much padding the label gets
Which corner radius the component should have
test.explain: Behaviour is what the guide must specify.
